title: Section XI. Of a particular Providence and of a future State
author: David Hume
summary: In a dialogue with a friend who speaks for Epicurus, Hume argues that from the order of the world we can infer a cause only as great as the effect shows, and never a providence or a future state of rewards and punishments beyond what we already see.

notes.on: the banishment of Protagoras, and the death of Socrates
notes.note: Protagoras (c. 490–c. 420 BC), the sophist, was said to have been expelled from Athens for impiety; Socrates was condemned to death there in 399 BC.
Epicurus (341–270 BC) founded his school, the Garden, at Athens in about 307 BC. Hume's notes in this passage cite Lucian and the historian Cassius Dio.

notes.on: the wisest of all the Roman emperors
notes.note: Marcus Aurelius (emperor 161–180), who endowed chairs at Athens for each of the main schools of philosophy.

notes.on: I come hither, O ye Athenians
notes.note: The friend speaks as Epicurus, defending himself before the people of Athens.
